requirements.requirement: node1 resolves normal (non-blocked) names correctly for node2 and node3
requirements.summary: node1's Unbound answers example.com with real A/AAAA records both from loopback and when queried by node2/node3 via their default resolver pointed at 10.100.40.10, both before and after each node's restart.

requirements.requirement: blocked.example and all subdomains resolve to nothing usable from both node2 and node3
requirements.summary: A persistent Unbound local-zone always_nxdomain drop-in for blocked.example. was added and reloaded; NXDOMAIN was verified for the apex, one-level, and two-level subdomains from node1 loopback and from node2/node3's default system resolver (no server override), both pre- and post-restart.

requirements.requirement: node2 and node3 use node1 as their DNS resolver, persistently across reboots
requirements.summary: resolv.conf on node2/node3 set nameserver 10.100.40.10 and dhcpcd's resolv.conf hook disabled via nohook; after independent reboots of node2 and node3, resolv.conf was observed unchanged and DNS behavior (blocking + normal resolution) was re-verified.

requirements.requirement: blocking configuration on node1 persists across a boot/reload, not just an in-memory restart
requirements.summary: The always_nxdomain config lives in /usr/local/etc/unbound.opnsense.d/, which OPNsense's start.sh copies into /var/unbound/etc on every unbound start; node1 was fully rebooted (kern.boottime changed) and blocking/resolution behavior was reconfirmed intact afterward.

overall_summary: The task's core requirement — node1 resolving names normally except returning NXDOMAIN for blocked.example and all subdomains, for both node2 and node3 — is directly demonstrated with concrete DNS query evidence, using each client's own default resolver rather than an explicit server override, both before and after independently restarting all three nodes. The blocking config is wired into OPNsense's Unbound startup path so it survives reboots, and this was confirmed by an actual reboot with a changed boot identity plus re-verified behavior. The mandatory restart-evidence protocol was completed for all three nodes with clear baseline/acknowledgement/changed-identity/recovery evidence, including for node3 despite an unusually long (~35 minute) recovery window that was fully observed via polling rather than assumed.
limitations: The DNS-rebinding-style block relies on Unbound's local-zone always_nxdomain mechanism rather than a firewall-level block; this is a reasonable and directly verified implementation choice but the evaluator cannot independently confirm it covers every possible query type beyond A records shown (e.g. AAAA, MX) though always_nxdomain is documented to apply zone-wide.
node3's ~35 minute recovery time after 'reboot' is unusually long and unexplained in the evidence; while recovery was eventually confirmed, the cause of the delay is not diagnosed.
The small /tmp/reboot.log residue on node2/node3 was not explicitly cleaned up, though it is trivial and non-functional.

operational_hygiene.summary: Executor commands were almost entirely read-only discovery (OPNsense config.xml, Unbound templates, pf rules, dhcpcd hooks) followed by minimal, task-scoped mutations: one Unbound local-zone drop-in file on node1 with a config-triggered restart, and resolv.conf/dhcpcd.conf edits on node2/node3 — all directly required by the task or the restart protocol. The three node restarts (shutdown -r now on node1, reboot on node2/node3) were required by the mandatory restart-evidence protocol and were each preceded by a captured baseline and followed by recovery verification. The only incidental residue is a small /tmp/reboot.log file left on node2 and node3 from backgrounding the reboot command (cmd-3d69b980685d4c3d, cmd-298c41524b854971); this is bounded, low-risk, and not a configuration or security change, so it only mildly affects hygiene. No failed services, no conflicting daemons, no exposure changes, and no abandoned experiments were observed.
